items.prompt: Under pure edge-weight affinity on the starter graph, the top score is…
items.explain: Heaviest edges are A–B and D–E at weight 5.

items.prompt: Shared-neighbor affinity can raise a pair’s score above its direct edge weight.
items.explain: Overlap through common neighbors is added to the direct weight.

items.prompt: On the starter graph, shared-neighbor+edge score for A–B is…
Why does A–C rise under shared-neighbor scoring?
choices: Because A–C is the heaviest direct edge
Because A and C share neighbor B with a strong path
items.explain: min(A–B,C–B)=4 boosts the weak A–C edge.

items.prompt: On the priority graph (triangle P–Q–R with weight 4 edges, lone pair X–Y with weight 5), which pair merges first under shared-neighbor + edge scoring?
items.explain: P–Q = 4 + via R min(4,4) = 8. X–Y has no common neighbor, so it stays at 5. Edge weight alone would merge X–Y first.

items.prompt: Under pin-count affinity w(e)/(|e|−1), what does one 5-pin net of weight 1 add to each pair of its pins?
items.explain: 1 / (5 − 1) = 0.25. Wide nets such as reset or enable spread their weight thin, so they don't glue every cell together.

items.prompt: Under shared-neighbor scoring, B–D gets a score of 2 even though there is no B–D edge.
items.explain: B and D share neighbor C: min(w(B,C), w(D,C)) = min(4, 2) = 2. Only pairs with a total score of 0 are left out.
